entry.summary:
Source: @fazelimohammadir

Give the gasoline to the people: fixing the imbalance with quota certificates. Sadegh Al-Hosseini argues that all the solutions proposed by the Ministry of Oil, the Plan and Budget Organization, and other solutions offered by others are inefficient and have more side effects compared to a plan based on giving an equal share of subsidized gasoline to all people. Watch the interview: https://youtu.be/4v6GxJolE9A. Al-Hosseini believes that by distributing an equal quota among all Iranians, based on a distribution of 90 million liters per day, and setting aside 30 million liters for working cars and motorcycles, the gasoline imbalance can be treated, and more importantly, an economic mechanism free from government intervention can be created to optimize equipment and energy consumers. In this detailed interview, he explains all aspects of his plan and finally addresses criticisms against the removal of the preferential exchange rate. This interview was recorded in response to Mohsen Yazdanpanah's critiques of the equal gasoline quota plan for everyone, which was previously published on IranTalk. Solutions to the Iran-US conflict: from a national doctrine to redefining power. Sahand Iranmehr is an expert in international relations and foreign policy, although he is better known as a literary author. In this conversation, he examines the history of the Iran-US conflict from the Pahlavi era to the present day to reach the complexities of this relationship and show why this relationship can only be managed through a gradual process. Watch the conversation: https://youtu.be/G4p9D-CB28A. Sahand Iranmehr believes that the recent wars between the two countries have created grounds for different perceptions of the two countries' situations relative to each other, and despite all the mistrust, grounds have been created to move past tension and gradually move toward a state of conflict containment and competition management. He offers various solutions, including presenting a national doctrine to redefining power, as solutions for managing the Iran-US conflict. Critical ConversationsMohammad FazeliFor a society that has experienced the bloody and catastrophic events of Aban 98 (November 2019), dialogue about any plan related to changing gasoline and energy policy is vital. For a society where the energy imbalance has reached a life-or-death threshold, dialogue about any plan related to changing gasoline and energy policy is vital. The conversation with Dr. Mohsen Yazdanpanah, an economist, published on the Iran Talk media outlet under the title "Gasoline Reforms: Without Fireworks," was an attempt to open a dialogue about the plan some in the government are pursuing, critique it, and show its consequences.Watching "Gasoline Reforms: Without Fireworks" — any plan can be critiqued, including the current government's plan; and any critique can also be critiqued, including the critiques Mohsen Yazdanpanah levels at the current plan. What matters is that for any chronic and complex issue—such as energy in today's Iran—there is no better path than policy transparency, social dialogue, and building social and political consensus on the best solutions. All those interested in energy policy and debates on price and non-price reforms in gasoline and other energy carriers can be invited to watch this conversation and join the social debate about it. These are critical conversations.

👆According to Note 3 of Article 27, "Producing artistic work without a permit from the country's legal institutions will result in six months to five years of prohibition from artistic activity and two to four times the production costs of the work." Of course, this does not mean that, for example, "if you paint a picture at home, you must first obtain a permit from the country's legal institutions," but the way it is written is so unprofessional that it allows for abuse and expansion of the concept of crime. The same applies to the very broad phrase "under the support, supervision, guidance, training, or direction of a foreign agent," under which anything can be interpreted as criminal. This scope is so wide that even repenting for a crime not committed becomes a crime; does the scripture of judgment and governance have no verse of mercy? The implementation of such a plan and the restrictions on independent internet media such as "Azad" completely eliminates the intermediate class of intellectual elites, takes political struggle to the blind instincts of the yellow layers of society, and drives the masses to the same place we saw in the bitter tragedies of Dey 1404. When you push honorable artists and intellectuals out of the arena with flimsy excuses, the way opens for those who win awards at international festivals by producing yellow and dark-portraying films and artistic works that misrepresent Iran's image. A class of yellow intellectuals and undereducated celebrities, through self-display, become hollow heroes for naive youth. The end result is clear; the enemies create sedition from "insubordination" and "weapons," and again you portray an inhuman image of Iran and the Islamic Republic, and before world public opinion, you become apologists for the warmongering of enemies. That's it.

America from Within: The Sociology of the Iran-US Conflict
Dr. Mahmoud Sadri, an Iranian sociologist living in the United States with fifty years of experience living, researching, and teaching in American society and universities, discusses the inner characteristics of American society, the role of political currents, extremist religious movements, and social forces in shaping US policy toward Iran. Watch the interview: https://youtu.be/G5WkWgwBKIM

Mahmoud Sadri believes there is no irreconcilable structural conflict of interests in Iran-US relations and that with more reasonable behavior and a bit of historical luck, relations between Iran and the US can be improved. He argues that actions known as extremism serve no benefit to Iran's national interests and only strengthen the discourse of anti-Iranian extremists in America. He also believes Iran suffers greatly from a lack of proper public diplomacy and absence of voice in American society and politics, to the extent that Iran-hatred is cost-free for everyone in the US.
